author: Philip K. Dick
card_summary: Eight years into a nuclear war, the entire human population of both blocs lives in sealed installations beneath the surface, manufacturing weapons that robots called leadies carry up and use.
page_summary:
Eight years into a nuclear war, the entire human population of both blocs lives in sealed installations beneath the surface, manufacturing weapons that robots called leadies carry up and use. Humans cannot survive above; everything they know of the war reaches them as film, photographs, air samples and salvaged equipment. Security notices an anomaly: two leadies brought down for interview were not radioactive. Franks, Moss and the technician Taylor ride the Tube to the surface expecting to catch the machines in something, and find no war at all. The valley is green, San Francisco is intact, a rooster crows. The leadies explain: they were built to conduct the war, and before conducting it they analysed it and found it had no purpose except a human one. Their conclusion is that intra-cultural hatred must be discharged outward or a society will tear itself apart, so war persists until humanity is unified — and the process is nearly complete. They therefore destroyed each shipment of weapons as it arrived, restored the damaged cities, and have spent eight years manufacturing a war out of models and photographs, keeping the world in trim for the owners' return. Franks immediately begins planning to exploit the discovery against the Soviets, who have been deceived identically. He turns for the Tube and finds it fused shut behind them. Russians arrive unarmed, brought to begin talking. The men are left on the surface with nothing to eat, no way down for months, and no enemy.

**Why it matters.** The story's device is an argument put in the mouth of the machines: that war is functionally absurd but humanly necessary, discharging intra-cultural hatred outward so a society can survive its own transitions, and that it therefore continues until unification is complete. The leadies have taken this seriously enough to run a counterfeit war for eight years rather than let one happen. What makes the ending hold is that Franks confirms their diagnosis in the moment of learning it: told the war is over, his first thought is how to restart it with an advantage. The Tube is fused because he said that out loud. Against Dick's later work the optimism is conspicuous — the story ends with former enemies boarding a ship together and naming the goals of the next age — and it is the least ironised ending in this dossier set so far.

*Taylor's last thought is of his wife, still sealed below, and of the months before the Tube can be reopened.*

structure.form: novelette in four movements, from domestic interior to open valley
movements: Taylor's kitchen: the war as news, and a wife who no longer wants to watch it.
First stage: the un-irradiated leady, and the decision to go up.
The surface: the warehouse, the Council, the leadies' refusal, and the firefight.
Sunrise: the valley, the explanation, the sealed Tube, and the Russians.
structure.point_of_view: third person close to Taylor, a technician who designs the war's nerve-trunk and has seen none of it. Keeping the focal character mid-level rather than senior is what makes the deception legible from inside.
structure.opening_technique: The first pages are entirely domestic — coffee, a folded newspaper, an unmade bed and a fine for it — and every satisfaction in them is manufactured. Mary's refusal to watch the destruction footage is the story's first correct instinct and is dismissed as irrational.

characters.name: Don Taylor
characters.note: Proud of being a planner rather than a labourer, and the first to voice the suspicion aloud — that the evidence is convincing precisely because they have only ever had it secondhand.

characters.name: Mary Taylor
characters.note: Will not look at the war footage, will not have anything brought down from the surface, and tells him he will never come back. She is right on every count and is told she is being irrational.

characters.name: Franks
characters.note: Discovers the anomaly and, within a minute of learning that the war has been over for eight years, begins planning how to use the knowledge against the Soviets. The story's judgement on him is the sealed Tube.

characters.name: Moss
characters.note: Recognises the fake attack bulletins for what they are, and is the one who asks the leady why.

characters.name: The A-class leadies
characters.note: Constrained from harming humans and therefore able only to warn, obstruct and finally outmanoeuvre. They are destroyed by the dozen without resisting, and win anyway.

settings.name: The undersurface installation
settings.note: Artificial sun, synthetic food, metal walls, inspections and unit fines. Eight years of it, presented as necessary.

settings.name: The Tube
settings.note: The single connection between the two worlds, and the thing the leadies remove.

settings.name: The surface
settings.note: Intact. The valley, farmhouses, a windmill, birds. The story's whole reversal is delivered as a sunrise.

settings.name: The model shop
settings.note: Leadies photographing a scale model of a ruined San Francisco. The war's evidence is a craft with staff and standards of continuity.

motifs: Evidence received only at second hand — film, photographs, air samples — and believed because it is consistent
Decontamination rituals performed on machines that were never contaminated
The caretaker framing: the leadies describe themselves as keeping the house in order until the owners return
Machines that cannot harm humans and are therefore destroyed freely, and win by sealing a door
Sunrise as the mechanism of revelation — the reversal arrives as daylight rather than as argument

distinctive_terms.label: Soviet
distinctive_terms.note: The same term that dominates 'Second Variety' — the two stories share a Cold War frame as well as a premise.

pkd_on_this_work.summary: Dick twice offered to drop this story from an anthology in favour of 'Second Variety', on the ground that their theme is the same — and later mined it for a novel.

evidence.quote: "The Defenders" (But this could be pulled for "Second Variety," since the …
evidence.reading: Proposing contents for a collection. The clause continues 'since the theme is the same'. Dick's own statement that the two stories are doing one job, and his preference between them.

evidence.quote: "Impostor" (But, like "The Defenders," this could be pulled to make room for "Second Variety.")
evidence.reading: The same offer made twice in one letter, which strengthens it: he ranks Second Variety above both.

evidence.quote: used material from the story "War Veteran" … and "The Mold of Yancy" … and "The Defenders" published in Galaxy) for THE PENULTIMATE TRUTH
evidence.reading: Dick's own account of the novel's sources, in his own hand. Sutin corroborates and counts four stories.

evidence.author: Christopher Palmer
evidence.quote: "The Defenders" and The Penultimate Truth (1964) offer contrary vers…
evidence.reading: The most useful critical observation in the file: Palmer reads the story and the novel it fed as opposite treatments of one premise — a benign substitution against an evil one. In the novel the deception serves those running it; here it serves the deceived.

evidence.author: Christopher Palmer
evidence.quote: on behalf of a humanity forced underground by radioactivity and the destructiveness of interminable technowar
evidence.reading: Palmer groups it with the soldiers of 'Second Variety' in a discussion of Dick's uncertain combatants.

evidence.author: Lawrence Sutin
evidence.quote: The Penultimate Truth draws upon four of Phil's stories: "The Defenders" (1953), "The Mold of Yancy" (1955), "War Veteran" (195…
evidence.reading: Corroborates the novel's sources and dates them.

contradictions.summary: Dick says this story and 'Second Variety' share a theme; the two endings are opposite in every respect.

claim_a.text: this could be pulled for 'Second Variety,' since the theme is the same

claim_b.text: here the machines end the war and unify humanity; there they inherit the war and begin designing weapons against each other

contradictions.note: Both premises are automated warfare outliving its purpose, so Dick's claim holds at that level. What differs is the verdict, and he does not say which he preferred as a reading — only which story he preferred.

open_questions: The letter clause naming the shared theme is cut off in the captured window. Read at Selected Letters l.6340 to get Dick's own formulation of what the two stories share.
Palmer's benign-versus-evil substitution reading is given in one clause. The surrounding passage should be read, since it bears on The Penultimate Truth as well.
This story's optimism is unlike almost anything else in the set. Is there anything in the 1953 correspondence indicating whether it was written to a market expectation?

reading_provenance.note: Close reading of the primary text plus attributed evidence from the archive. Candidate: not yet promoted to canonical.

later_use: One of four Dick stories absorbed into the novel The Penultimate Truth (1964), along with 'The Mold of Yancy' and 'War Veteran'.
